prime.problem: Writing a backward pass by hand for a whole network gives you 26 gradients and one loss. If any one is wrong, training quietly gets worse, and nothing tells you which line broke.
prime.fits: This is the setup for all of Exercise 1. It reuses Lecture 4's MLP with BatchNorm and the micrograd idea that every intermediate has a gradient; now each intermediate becomes a named tensor you can check against PyTorch.
prime.goal: Split a forward pass into checkable steps, make PyTorch keep every intermediate gradient, and read cmp's three verdicts to tell a real bug from rounding.

attend: Why does splitting F.cross_entropy into eight lines make a backward bug easier to locate, not just easier to write?
Which tensors does PyTorch keep .grad for by default, and what does retain_grad() change?
When should exact: False worry you, and when is approximate: True enough?
How can initialising bngain to exactly 1 make a wrong gradient pass the check?

must: Forward pass split into ~20 named tensors → each has its own .grad from autograd → you can check each hand-written d<name> the moment you write it → a mistake is pinned to one line instead of surfacing twenty lines later in dW1

PyTorch frees intermediate gradients to save memory → t.grad is None for non-leaf tensors → retain_grad() on all 19 intermediates before loss.backward() → autograd becomes an answer key for every step
Same math in a different order → float32 rounds differently (~1e-9) → exact can be False for a correct formula → trust allclose (1e-8 + 1e-5·|x|) and a tiny maxdiff; only approximate: False is a bug

Init of exactly 1 or 0 → multiplying by 1 or adding 0 changes nothing → a gradient that forgot that factor still matches (dbnraw = dhpreact is exact: True) → small random inits make the bug show (maxdiff 0.0017)
elevated: counts_sum**-1 rather than 1.0/counts_sum → autograd's backward for the power op matches the hand formula bit for bit → exact: True instead of maxdiff 9.3e-10
reference: the cmp print format ({s:15s} | exact: … | approximate: … | maxdiff: …)
the exact retain_grad list and its order
parameter shapes: C (27, 10), W1 (30, 64), W2 (64, 27); 4,137 in total
the loss 3.3377 in the video vs 3.3444 in the lab (unseeded bngain/bnbias draw)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how Karpathy sets up Exercise 1 so that every hand-written gradient can be checked. Or draw the pipeline: chunked forward → retain_grad → backward → cmp, and write under each box what goes wrong if you skip it.
checklist: the forward pass is rewritten as ~20 atomic tensors (19 intermediates plus loss), one operation each
retain_grad() makes PyTorch keep .grad on the intermediates; one loss.backward() fills all 26
exact: False with approximate: True is rounding, not a bug
biases and BatchNorm parameters get small random inits so a missing factor can't hide

retrieve.q: Explain why a gradient checker needs the intermediate gradients and not only the 7 parameter gradients.
answer: parameter gradients only say that something is wrong somewhere upstream
intermediate gradients let you check each step as you write it
so the first failing cmp line names the broken formula

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens when you call cmp('logprobs', dlogprobs, logprobs): where t.grad came from, and what each of the three printed values computes.
answer: logprobs.retain_grad() was called before loss.backward(), so autograd stored its gradient in logprobs.grad
exact: torch.all(dt == t.grad), every entry bit-equal
approximate: torch.allclose, each entry within 1e-8 + 1e-5·|t.grad|
maxdiff: the largest absolute difference over all 864 entries

retrieve.q: You add 2e-8 to every entry of a correct dlogprobs. Is it approximate? Would you rather the checker were stricter or looser, and what does each choice cost?
answer: approximate: False: most entries are 0, where only atol = 1e-8 of slack applies
stricter (exact only) flags correct formulas that merely reorder float32 math
looser tolerances let small real bugs through, like a missing factor close to 1

retrieve.q: Your dbnraw prints exact: True, but training later diverges. Name one way the checker itself could have misled you.
answer: an init of exactly 1 (bngain) or 0 hides a missing multiply or add
the check passes for this batch and init but the formula is still wrong in general
fix: randomise those parameters and re-check

compare.q: In micrograd you checked your Value gradients against PyTorch too. What is fundamentally different about checking at tensor level, and what new way of failing appears?
answer: micrograd compared a handful of scalars; here each check covers a whole tensor (up to 32×64 entries)
at tensor level you need a verdict over many entries: exact vs allclose vs maxdiff
new failure: shapes and broadcasting, so a gradient can have the right values in the wrong shape, or pass only because of a special init

compare.q: The atomic backward through cross-entropy checks exact: True; the three-line analytic dlogits only gets approximate: True. Which design choice causes the difference, and when would you pick each?
answer: atomic: same operations in the same order as autograd, so bit-identical
analytic: a simplified formula, so rounding differs (maxdiff about 1e-8)
pick atomic to learn and debug one step at a time; analytic to train fast with less memory
atomic fails by being long and easy to break; analytic fails silently if the derivation has an error and you don't check it

predict.q: You add one more intermediate to the forward pass but forget to put it in the retain_grad list. What does cmp do when you check its gradient?
predict.answer: It crashes rather than printing False. The tensor's .grad is None (PyTorch warns that you're reading .grad of a non-leaf tensor), so dt == t.grad is a plain Python False, and torch.all(False) raises a TypeError. An error you can't miss is better than a silent pass.

apply.task: In the lab, after the correct dlogprobs, add a constant eps to it for eps = 1e-9, 5e-9, 2e-8 and 1e-7, and call cmp on each. Before running, use the allclose rule (|dt − t.grad| ≤ 1e-8 + 1e-5·|t.grad|) to predict which ones are approximate: True. Remember 832 of the 864 true entries are exactly 0.
apply.done: Your predictions match the run: 1e-9 and 5e-9 are approximate: True (maxdiff 1.86e-9 and 5.59e-9); 2e-8 and 1e-7 are approximate: False (maxdiff 2.05e-8 and 1.01e-7).
apply.hint: At a zero entry, rtol adds nothing, so the only slack is atol = 1e-8.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the bngain = 1 bug being invisible, or the 1.86e-9 instead of 1e-9?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why retain_grad is needed, or why exact and approximate disagree?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: special init → hidden bug, or float32 rounding → exact: False?
Before the softmax card, can you say which of the 26 gradients you expect to need two branches?
Would you trust a backward pass that passed cmp on one batch? What else would you check?
